Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- The House of Representatives on Tuesday passed a bill that would make suing for pay discrimination easier by altering a time limit on such suits. The act is named for Lilly Ledbetter, seen here in 2008. Her discrimination lawsuit victory was overturned in 2007. The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which passed 250-177, would give workers alleging unequal pay the right to sue within 180 days of their most recent paycheck. Current law says such employees must sue within 180 days of receiving their first unfair paycheck. Supporters of the new legislation say that, under the current law, an employer merely needs to hide unfair pay practices for three months before being able to continue them without penalty. The act, named for a former Goodyear Tire employee who sued the company for gender discrimination in 1998, would effectively overturn a 2007 Supreme Court decision on the limit. Ledbetter was awarded $360,000 in back pay by a federal judge in Alabama, but the verdict was overturned in a 5-4 Supreme Court ruling in May 2007. The court said that even though she filed her complaint within 180 days of when she first learned that she was getting paid less than comparable male employees, she had failed to file within 180 days of the first unequal paycheck. After Tuesday's House vote, Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the chamber had "taken a bold step" in passing the legislation. "In doing so, it has injected fairness, reason and common sense back into policy," Pelosi said. The legislation, which passed the Senate on Thursday, now goes to President Barack Obama, who has promised to sign it into law. It is the first major piece of legislation Congress has sent to Obama for his approval. On the campaign trail, Obama and Republican nominee Sen. John McCain debated the bill. Obama heavily emphasized what he called the plan's benefits to working women, while McCain criticized it as a boon for trial lawyers. Pelosi said Obama called to congratulate her on the bill's passage. Obama danced with Ledbetter at one of his inaugural balls, and she spoke at the Democrat National Convention at which he accepted his party's nomination. "My case is over -- I will never receive the pay I deserve," Ledbetter said in that speech. "But there will be a far richer reward if we secure fair pay for our children and grandchildren, so that no one will ever again experience the discrimination that I did."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Tuesday, the House of Representatives approved legislation changing the deadline for filing pay-discrimination lawsuits, making it easier for employees to bring such claims.

The measure, called the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, passed by a vote of 250-177. It would allow workers who believe they received unequal pay to file suit within 180 days of their latest paycheck. Under existing law, the 180-day period begins when an employee receives the first discriminatory paycheck.

Advocates for the bill argue that the current rule enables employers to avoid consequences simply by concealing discriminatory compensation practices for three months.

The legislation is named after Lilly Ledbetter, a former Goodyear Tire employee who sued the company for gender discrimination in 1998. Ledbetter, pictured in 2008, initially won her case, but that victory was reversed in 2007.

An Alabama federal judge awarded her $360,000 in back pay. However, in May 2007, the Supreme Court overturned the decision in a 5-4 ruling. The justices concluded that although Ledbetter filed her complaint within 180 days of discovering that she earned less than comparable male employees, she had not acted within 180 days of receiving her first unequal paycheck.

The new law would, in effect, reverse the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the filing deadline.

Following the House vote, Speaker Nancy Pelosi described the bill’s passage as a “bold step,” saying lawmakers had restored “fairness, reason and common sense” to public policy.

The Senate approved the legislation on Thursday, and it now heads to President Barack Obama, who has pledged to sign it. It is the first significant bill Congress has submitted to Obama for approval.

During the presidential campaign, Obama and Republican nominee Sen. John McCain disagreed over the proposal. Obama strongly promoted what he described as its advantages for working women, while McCain argued that it would primarily benefit trial attorneys.

Pelosi said Obama telephoned her to offer congratulations after the measure passed. Obama also danced with Ledbetter at one of his inaugural balls. Earlier, she had addressed the Democratic National Convention where he accepted the party’s presidential nomination.

In that speech, Ledbetter acknowledged that her own case had ended and that she would never obtain the compensation she believed she was owed. She added, however, that ensuring equal pay for future generations would provide an even greater reward by preventing others from enduring the discrimination she experienced.

**House passes bill easing deadline for pay discrimination claims**

**WASHINGTON —** The House voted Friday to make it easier for workers to challenge pay discrimination, approving legislation that would restart the deadline for filing a claim each time an employee receives a discriminatory paycheck.

The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act passed January 9, 2009, by a vote of 247-171. It was named for Lilly Ledbetter, a former Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. employee who said she was paid less than male colleagues doing similar work.

The measure responds to a 2007 Supreme Court ruling that rejected Ledbetter’s lawsuit. The court ruled that under federal law, she should have filed a complaint within 180 days of the company’s original discriminatory pay decision—even though she said she did not learn of the disparity until years later.

Under the House-approved bill, the filing period would begin again whenever a worker receives compensation affected by discrimination. That means each unequal paycheck could count as a new violation, giving employees 180 days to file a claim—or 300 days in jurisdictions where the longer federal deadline applies.

Supporters said the change recognizes that salaries are often confidential and that workers may not immediately know they are being paid less because of their sex, race, religion, national origin, age or disability.

“Each paycheck that delivers discriminatory pay is a wrong that should be subject to challenge,” Democratic supporters argued during debate.

Opponents, including many Republicans and business groups, warned that the legislation could expose employers to lawsuits over compensation decisions made years or decades earlier, when records and witnesses may no longer be available.

Ledbetter worked at a Goodyear plant in Alabama for nearly two decades before discovering that she was earning less than several male supervisors. A jury initially awarded her damages, but the Supreme Court’s 5-4 decision said her complaint had been filed too late.

The legislation now heads to the Senate. President-elect Barack Obama has said he supports the measure, making it likely to become one of the first bills he signs after taking office.

## House votes 250–177 to overturn Ledbetter pay-discrimination ruling

**Washington, Jan. 27, 2009** — The House voted 250–177 to give final congressional approval to the **Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**, legislation reversing a 2007 Supreme Court decision that sharply limited when workers may bring pay-discrimination claims.

The bill provides that the legal filing period begins again each time an employee receives a paycheck affected by a discriminatory compensation decision. It responds directly to the Supreme Court’s 5–4 ruling in *Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.*, which held that Ledbetter should have filed her complaint within 180 days of the original discriminatory pay decision—even though she said she did not learn for years that male colleagues were being paid more.

Ledbetter, a former Goodyear supervisor in Alabama, argued that every reduced paycheck perpetuated the discrimination. The new legislation adopts that position and applies it to claims under federal laws prohibiting discrimination based on sex, race, age, disability and other protected characteristics.

The vote was largely along party lines, with most Democrats supporting the measure and most Republicans opposing it. Supporters said employees often cannot discover salary discrimination before the filing deadline because compensation information is confidential. Opponents warned that restarting the deadline with every paycheck could expose employers to lawsuits over decisions made many years earlier, when records and witnesses may no longer be available.

The Senate had approved the measure 61–36. President Barack Obama, who supported the legislation during his campaign, was expected to sign it, making it the first bill enacted under his administration. The act would apply to discriminatory compensation claims pending on or after May 28, 2007, the day before the Supreme Court issued its Ledbetter decision.

**BREAKING NEWS: Congress Sends Obama Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**

**WASHINGTON, Jan. 27, 2009** — Congress on Tuesday sent President Barack Obama the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, the first major legislation of his presidency and a significant victory for advocates of equal pay and workers’ rights.

The House gave final approval to the bill, which reverses a 2007 Supreme Court decision that sharply limited when employees may challenge pay discrimination. Obama has said he will sign the measure.

The legislation clarifies that the deadline for filing a pay-discrimination claim resets with each discriminatory paycheck, rather than beginning only when an employer first makes the discriminatory pay decision.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi praised the vote as a major step toward ensuring that women and other workers can seek redress for unequal pay. She said it was fitting that fair-pay legislation would be the first bill sent to the new president, calling equal pay a matter of fairness for American families.

The measure is named for Lilly Ledbetter, a former Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. supervisor who learned near the end of her career that she had been paid less than male colleagues doing similar work. The Supreme Court ruled that she had filed her complaint too late, even though she said she had not discovered the disparity until years after it began.

Ledbetter, who watched lawmakers take up her cause after losing her own claim, hailed the bill as a victory for workers who may not immediately know they are being underpaid.

“This bill is not just about me,” Ledbetter said. “It is about all the women and others who are being paid less than they deserve and may not know it.”

The legislation does not award Ledbetter back pay or reopen her case. Instead, it changes federal law for future claims under several anti-discrimination statutes.

Obama’s expected signature will mark the completion of a two-year effort by congressional Democrats to overturn the Supreme Court ruling. Then-President George W. Bush had threatened to veto an earlier version of the measure.

# How a Goodyear Manager’s Lawsuit Reshaped U.S. Pay-Discrimination Law

**WASHINGTON —** The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, the first bill signed into law by President Barack Obama, grew out of a narrow Supreme Court ruling with broad consequences: When does the clock begin to run for an employee challenging discriminatory pay?

For Lilly Ledbetter, a longtime supervisor at a Goodyear tire plant in Alabama, the answer determined whether she could seek redress for years of allegedly lower pay. For Congress, the case became a larger argument over workplace equality, statutes of limitations, stale claims and the proper roles of courts and lawmakers.

The resulting statute did not create a general guarantee of equal pay or automatically prove that any wage disparity was discriminatory. Instead, it changed the rules governing when certain pay-discrimination claims may be filed. Under the law, each paycheck or other compensation affected by a discriminatory decision can restart the period for bringing a charge.

Supporters described the measure as a practical response to the secrecy that often surrounds salaries. Opponents warned that it would expose employers to litigation over decisions made years earlier, after records had disappeared and witnesses’ memories had faded.

## A career shadowed by a pay gap

Ledbetter began working for Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. in 1979 at its plant in Gadsden, Alabama. She was one of relatively few women in a predominantly male management workforce.

Near the end of her career, Ledbetter learned that she was earning less than many male managers performing similar work. She alleged that discriminatory evaluations and raises earlier in her employment had compounded over time, leaving her with substantially lower compensation.

Ledbetter filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and sued Goodyear under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Title VII prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin. Before going to court under that law, an employee generally must file an administrative charge within 180 days of the alleged unlawful employment practice, or within 300 days in jurisdictions where a state or local agency enforces a similar law.

A federal jury sided with Ledbetter and awarded back pay and damages. The award was later reduced under statutory limits, and Goodyear continued to contest the claim.

The company argued that the relevant decisions setting Ledbetter’s pay had been made outside the filing period. Ledbetter countered that every paycheck reflecting the earlier discrimination constituted a new violation.

## The Supreme Court’s 5-to-4 decision

In **Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.**, decided on May 29, 2007, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 against Ledbetter.

Writing for the majority, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. said the time limit generally began when the allegedly discriminatory pay decision was made and communicated—not each time the employee later received a paycheck affected by that decision. The majority relied on earlier cases distinguishing a present discriminatory act from the continuing effects of a past act.

Under that interpretation, Ledbetter could not rely on pay-setting decisions made outside the statutory filing window unless she could identify a discriminatory decision within the window itself. The issuance of a paycheck, the majority concluded, did not by itself restart the clock when the paycheck merely carried forward the effects of an earlier decision.

The ruling focused on filing deadlines, not on whether Ledbetter had in fact been paid less because of her sex. The Court did not hold that unequal pay was lawful. It held that her Title VII claim had not been brought within the required period.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg delivered a dissent from the bench, an unusual step that underscored the depth of disagreement. Joined by Justices John Paul Stevens, David Souter and Stephen Breyer, she argued that pay discrimination often develops gradually and can be difficult for employees to detect.

“Pay disparities often occur, as they did in Ledbetter’s case, in small increments,” Ginsburg wrote. Employees may not know what colleagues earn, she observed, and workplace culture may discourage discussion of salaries. She urged Congress to correct what she considered the majority’s unduly restrictive reading of Title VII.

The dissent helped turn a technical procedural dispute into a national political cause.

## What Congress changed

Congress responded with legislation named for Ledbetter. After an unsuccessful effort in 2008, the measure passed soon after Democrats expanded their congressional majorities and Obama entered the White House.

The House approved the final bill by a vote of **250 to 177**, and the Senate passed it **61 to 36**. Obama signed it on Jan. 29, 2009, with Ledbetter present.

The law states that an unlawful employment practice involving compensation occurs when:

- A discriminatory compensation decision or practice is adopted;
- An employee becomes subject to that decision or practice; or
- An employee is affected by its application, including each time wages, benefits or other compensation are paid.

In practical terms, if an earlier discriminatory decision continues to reduce a worker’s current paycheck, receipt of that paycheck can begin a new filing period.

The statute amended the compensation-discrimination provisions associated with several federal laws, including:

- **Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964;**
- **The Age Discrimination in Employment Act;**
- **The Americans with Disabilities Act;** and
- **The Rehabilitation Act.**

It applies not only to salary and hourly wages but potentially to bonuses, pension contributions and other forms of compensation when they are affected by a discriminatory decision or practice.

Congress made the act effective as if enacted on May 28, 2007—the day before the Supreme Court’s Ledbetter decision—and applied it to claims pending on or after that date.

## What the law did not do

Despite its political symbolism, the act made a targeted procedural change.

It did not eliminate the requirement that workers file charges with the EEOC promptly after receiving a discriminatory paycheck or other covered compensation. Rather, it clarified that each affected payment may constitute a new unlawful employment practice.

It also did not guarantee that a worker will win a case. A plaintiff must still prove that the compensation disparity resulted from unlawful discrimination. Employers may defend pay differences based on experience, performance, seniority, productivity, job duties, market conditions or other lawful factors.

The act did not remove Title VII’s limits on available damages. Nor did it permit unlimited recovery for decades of past pay. Under the statute, back pay based on earlier compensation decisions may generally be recovered for up to two years before the filing of an EEOC charge, when the earlier acts are similar or related to the practice occurring within the filing period.

The measure also should not be confused with the **Equal Pay Act of 1963**, which separately prohibits sex-based wage disparities between employees performing substantially equal work, subject to specified defenses. The Ledbetter law principally concerns when claims accrue under federal anti-discrimination statutes.

## The case for the legislation

Democrats, civil-rights organizations, labor unions and women’s advocacy groups argued that the Supreme Court’s rule failed to reflect how compensation decisions work.

Unlike a firing or a refusal to hire—events that are usually obvious—pay discrimination may remain hidden. Many workplaces discourage employees from discussing compensation, and workers may not discover discrepancies until years after an initial salary decision or performance evaluation.

Supporters also emphasized the cumulative nature of pay. A modest disparity in one raise can affect later percentage increases, bonuses and retirement benefits. In their view, each reduced paycheck is not simply a lingering consequence of an old decision but a renewed application of discrimination.

Obama presented the law as both an equality measure and an economic one, arguing that families suffer when workers are underpaid because of sex, race, age, disability or another protected characteristic.

Ledbetter herself became a prominent advocate, although the legislation could not restore her original jury award. The law changed the rules for other workers and pending cases; it did not reopen her concluded lawsuit.

## The case against it

Republicans and business organizations generally agreed that intentional pay discrimination should be illegal but disputed the legislation’s approach to deadlines.

Opponents said statutes of limitations serve an important purpose: encouraging prompt claims while evidence is still available. If each paycheck renews the filing period, they argued, employers may have to defend decisions made by supervisors who have retired or died, using records that were lawfully discarded years earlier.

Some critics characterized the bill as a boon to trial lawyers and warned that it would increase litigation costs. They favored alternatives that would have allowed extra time when an employee could not reasonably have discovered the discrimination, rather than automatically treating every paycheck as a new violation.

Business groups also raised questions about how broadly courts might interpret a “compensation decision or other practice,” including whether decisions involving job assignments, evaluations or promotions could qualify when they later affected pay.

Supporters responded that the law still requires a timely charge tied to a current paycheck and still places the burden on the employee to prove discrimination. They also noted that back-pay recovery remains limited, reducing the threat of open-ended monetary liability.

## A political symbol with a precise legal purpose

The Ledbetter act arrived at a moment when equal-pay issues were becoming increasingly prominent in national politics. During the 2008 presidential campaign, Obama supported the measure, while Republican nominee Sen. John McCain opposed it and missed the Senate vote on an earlier version. The debate helped sharpen partisan differences over employment law, access to courts and federal regulation of the workplace.

Its enactment was celebrated as a major women’s-rights victory, although its legal reach extends beyond sex discrimination. Because it covers compensation claims under several civil-rights statutes, it can apply to allegations involving race, religion, national origin, age and disability as well.

The law’s central principle is straightforward: A discriminatory pay decision can be renewed when it is reflected in current compensation.

But the political dispute surrounding that principle remains familiar. One side sees the rule as essential because workers often cannot challenge hidden discrimination within months of the original decision. The other sees it as weakening the finality that filing deadlines are intended to provide.

More than a change in a calendar, the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act represented Congress’s rejection of the Supreme Court’s interpretation of when compensation discrimination occurs. It preserved short filing windows while ensuring that workers are not necessarily barred merely because the decision that first depressed their pay was made years before they learned of it.
